sources.label: California State Controller, By the Numbers: fiscal year 2023-24 Financial Transactions Report (revenues, expenditures, long-term debt and leases)
EFF Atlas of Surveillance (police surveillance technology, searched by department)

notes: Actual revenues and expenditures for fiscal year 2023-24 (ending June 30, 2024), as the city and county reported them to the State Controller. Not a budget.

Public schools are run by separate school districts, so they are not included. San Francisco is a consolidated city and county, so county services such as public health, social services and jails are included.
Water, sewer, electric, gas and solid waste utilities count as utilities; airports, ports and transit as infrastructure; public hospitals as health services.

Internal service funds (charges between departments), depreciation and transfers between funds are left out. Enterprise funds' interest is replaced by their principal and interest payments from the debt forms.
Courts, legal services, prosecutors and public defenders, housing, planning and community development count as overhead.
Debt is principal outstanding at year end on bonds, certificates of participation, other long-term debt, construction financing and leases, as reported.
Political money is not scored: California city candidates file campaign reports with their local filing officer, not with the state.
Transparency practices have not been checked yet, so they are not scored.

Red flags: surveillance programs come from the EFF Atlas of Surveillance, a public database of news reports and public records, searched on 2026-10-14. A town or county with none listed may still have programs nobody has reported. Data center deals, corporate tax breaks and license-plate cameras mapped by volunteers have not been checked for California yet. Most records carry no dollar amount, so each documented program costs a quarter of the red-flag points instead of being counted as spending.

redFlags.label: Real-time crime center
redFlags.detail: The San Francisco Police Department began operating a real-time crime center in 2024.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS017863, citing San Francisco Police Department website

redFlags.label: Police drones
redFlags.detail: The San Francisco Police Department implemented a drone program in 2024.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS013947, citing Mission Local

redFlags.label: License-plate readers
redFlags.detail: The San Francisco Police Department began installing 400 Flock Safety automated license plate readers across 100 intersections in 2024. Previously they contracted with Neology Pips.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS000909, citing NBC Bay Area

redFlags.label: Third-party investigative platform
redFlags.detail: The San Francisco Police Department transitioned from LexisNexis’ LexisNexis Accurint Virtual Crime Center investigative platform to Thomson Reuter’s CLEAR in 2023.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS013268, citing SF Police Department

redFlags.label: Predictive policing
redFlags.detail: The San Francisco Municipal Transit Authority acquired AISight predictive policing in 2012.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS009063, citing Slate

redFlags.label: Gunshot detection (ShotSpotter)
redFlags.detail: The San Francisco Police Department has been using Shotspotter gunshot detection technology since 2008.

source.label: EFF Atlas of Surveillance AOS004467, citing CNN
